# Asteroidal Triples and Friendsin (Likely Necessary) Matrix Multiplication Time

**Abstract**

In a seminal paper, Kratsch and Spinrad [SODA 2003 and SIAM Journal on Computing 2006] studied several important problems in structural graph theory that anticipated two trends in fine-grained complexity, both from the upper- and lower-bound side:

From the upper-bound side, for each of these problems the authors give an _intermediate_ running time strictly _between_ \(n^\omega\) _and n_<sup>3</sup>, where \(\omega<2.371177\) is the matrix multiplication exponent. When optimized, this running time can be made \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})\). By now, many more problems can be solved in this running time: directed unweighted or node-weighted APSP, a variety of matrix products such as max-min and dominance, RNA Folding and many more. For some of these, the community has also developed tools suggesting that this intermediate running time is necessary.

From the lower-bound side, the authors give lower bounds of \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\), conditioned on three natural hardness hypotheses on the complexity of quantified variants of triangle detection that account for different types of hardness of such problems.

Despite this, it has remained open for over 20 years which of these two pieces of evidence reflects the truth for the problems that Kratsch and Spinrad study: whether the intermediate running time is indeed necessary and stronger lower bounds hold, or whether the hardness evidence of Kratsch and Spinrad is essentially tight. In this paper, we resolve this question and show that the latter is the case: all problems admit an \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\) time algorithm.

As an additional contribution, we make partial algorithmic progress on further problems in structural graph theory of intermediate complexity, improving over previous work [Chiu and Lu, STACS 2022 and Information and Computation 2024][Spinrad, Discrete Applied Math 2004].

### 1 Introduction

Many problems in graph and matrix algorithms have natural cubic running times in terms of _n_, the number of nodes in the graph or the number of rows/columns of the matrices. For some perhaps infamous examples, such as All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) in weighted graphs, this cubic running time has persisted for many decades, except for _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> improvements, leading to conjectures that cubic time is the best possible (e.g.,[Vas18, WW10, VW18]). For other problems, substantial polynomial improvements have been obtained. The prime example for this is matrix multiplication. The exponent \(\omega\) is defined as the smallest real value for which \(n\times n\) matrices can be multiplied in \(\mathcal{O}(n^{\omega+\varepsilon})\) time for all \(\varepsilon>0\). It has been known since 1969 that \(\omega<3\) [Str69], and while the popular belief among computer scientists is that \(\omega=2\), the best known upper bound is \(\omega<2.371177\) [DEK<sup>+</sup>26].

Via reductions to matrix multiplication, a huge variety of problems have truly subcubic<sup>1</sup> time algorithms: many linear algebraic operations (matrix inverse, linear system solving, LUP decompositions and more), a variety of “funny” matrix products over other algebraic structures such as the max-min product of matrices [VWY09], many graph problems in unweighted graphs such as unweighted APSP [Zwi02, Sei95], structure similarity problems such as RNA-Folding [BGSV19], and many more.

<sup>1</sup> \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) time for constant \(\varepsilon>0\).

## 2 Asteroidal Triples and Friends in (Likely Necessary) Matrix Multiplication Time

There are simple reductions from Boolean matrix multiplication to many of these problems, showing that \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) time seems _necessary_ to solve them. This is true for instance for unweighted APSP and most "funny" matrix products. For even more problems, \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) time lower bounds can be proven under stronger but still plausible assumptions such as that detecting a triangle in an _n_-node graph requires \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) time. For problems with \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) time conditional lower bounds and subcubic time upper bounds using matrix multiplication, a natural question is:

_Can these problems be solved in_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\) _time or is there a higher conditional lower bound?_

The term "intermediate problem" has emerged to capture problems that are in truly subcubic time but whose running times are _strictly larger_ than \(n^\omega\). Several recent works study such problems within the context of fine-grained complexity \[BKPR19, LPV20, VX20a, CVX21, Fis26\], providing conditional lower bounds \(n^{c-o(1)}\) for \(c>\omega\) for some of these problems.

Most studied intermediate problems have running times that are \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{2.5})\) if \(\omega=2\); a popular running time is \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})\). This is the best known running time for the Dominance Product \[Mat91\], max- min matrix product and All-Pairs Bottleneck Paths \[VWY07, DP09\], All-Pairs Non-Decreasing Paths \[Vas10, DGZ18, DJW19\], Monotone Min-Plus Product \[BGSV19, VX20b, GPVX21, CDXZ22\], Language Edit Distance (also known as Scored Parsing \[AP72, Sah17, BGSV19\]), RNA Folding \[NJ80, Aku99, ZTZU11, VGF14, Sah17\], Dyck Edit Distance \[Sah14, BGSV19, DKS22, FGK<sup>+</sup>24\], Tree Edit Distance \[Mao21, Dür23, NPS<sup>+</sup>25\], Node-weighted APSP \[Cha10, Yus09, AFJ<sup>+</sup>25\], and Min-Equality Product \[VX20a\].

One of the very first papers to prove \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) lower bounds under plausible conjectures for a variety of graph problems, while also providing subcubic time algorithms using matrix multiplication, is a seminal SODA 2003 paper by Kratsch and Spinrad \[KS06\]. Almost all of the problems studied by \[KS06\] were solved in O(_n_<sup>2.79</sup>) time. With a small change<sup>2</sup> the algorithms can be made to run in \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})\) time. This motivates the following questions.

_Are these problems intermediate, or can they be solved in_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\) _time?_

_How do these problems fit into the recently established fine-grained hierarchy?_

Even the name of Kratsch and Spinrad’s paper "Between O(_mn_) and \(\mathcal{O}(n^\alpha)\)" (here \(\alpha=\omega\)) suggests that the problems in the paper are intermediate. Despite much recent progress on the fine-grained complexity of intermediate problems, the problems studied in Kratsch and Spinrad’s paper have not seen improvements since the paper was written more than 20 years ago.

The main contribution of our work is to show that these problems are not intermediate. They, in fact, admit conditionally tight \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\) time algorithms.

### 1.1 The problems studied by Kratsch and Spinrad

Kratsch and Spinrad \[KS06\] investigate the following algorithmic problems in structural graph theory that have very strong motivation, e.g., in the study of perfect graphs, AT-free graphs and triangulated graphs (see Appendix A for details). Given an (undirected) graph **G**=(_V,E_), the problems are:

\(\blacksquare\) Computing the _neighborhood-deleted components_ of **G**: Specifically, for each \(v\in V\) , compute the connected components of **G**\[_V_\\_N[v_\]\] (the graph obtained by removing _v_ and its neighborhood).

<sup>2</sup> The neighborhood connected components algorithm of \[KS06\] uses an inefficient way to list witnesses of Boolean matrix multiplication. Just by replacing Lemma 2.1 in \[KS06\] with the approach of \[AGMN92, GKL09\] to list up to _f_ witnesses per pair in \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(f\text{MM}(n,n/f,n))\) time, one obtains a running time \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(f\text{MM}(n,n/f,n)+\text{MM}(n,n^2/f,n))\) for neighborhood-deleted components which gives \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})\) via blocking or O(_n_<sup>2.616</sup>) with rectangular matrix multiplication. For the rest of the problems, in \[KS06\] there is an additional \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})\) cost after the neighborhood- deleted components are computed.

Listing or finding the _extremities_ of **G**: These are vertices \(v\in V\) such that **G**[_V_\\_N[v_]] is connected. This can be derived directly from the previous problem.

Determining whether **G** has a _star-cutset_ or a _clique-cutset_: A _cutset_ is a set of nodes \(S\subseteq V\) such that **G**[_V_\\_S_] is disconnected; it is a _star-cutset_ if there is a central node in _S_ connected to all other nodes in _S_, and a _clique-cutset_ if **G**[_S_] is a clique.

Recognizing _AT-free graphs_: This involves verifying whether **G** contains an _asteroidal triple_--an independent set of three vertices \(x,y,z\in V\) such that, between any two vertices in the triple, there exists a path avoiding the neighborhood of the third vertex.

Listing or finding _dominating pairs_: These are distinct nodes \(u,v\in V\) such that for every _u-v_ path \(\pi\) and every node \(w\in V\) , the path \(\pi\) contains at least one neighbor of _w_ or contains _w_ itself. (In other words, the vertex set of any path between these two vertices is a dominating set of the graph.)

Listing or finding _two-pairs_: These are distinct nodes \(u,v\in V\) such that all induced (or equivalently, chordless) paths between _u_ and _v_ have length two.

For all of these problems, the authors present algorithms with running times strictly _between_ O(_n_<sup>3</sup>) _and_ \(\mathcal{O}(n^\omega)\). Specifically, as mentioned earlier, an O(_n_<sup>2.79</sup>)-time algorithm is provided for all problems, except for recognizing AT-free graphs, which is solved in \(\mathcal{O}(n^{4\omega/(\omega+1)})=\mathcal{O}(n^{2.81})\) time. As mentioned earlier, the O(_n_<sup>2.79</sup>) time can be replaced by O(_n_<sup>2.69</sup>) by slightly modifying the algorithms. Prior to [KS06], only O(_nm_)-time algorithms were known for some of these problems, which still take \(\Omega(n^3)\) time on dense graphs.

## 1.2 Why \(n^\omega\) seems needed for all the problems

Spinrad and Kratsch provide evidence that solving the problems listed above requires at least \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) time. To support this, they identify three problems for which no algorithms faster than \(\mathcal{O}(n^\omega)\) are currently known (see Figure 1 for the hardness proven by [KS06] from these problems). For each of the three problems one hypothesizes that in the word-RAM model with _O_(log_n_) bit words, the problem requires \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) time.

**Determining whether a graph contains a triangle:** The corresponding Triangle Detection Hypothesis that the problem requires \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) time has been repeatedly used within fine-grained complexity (e.g., [Vas18, VW18, AV14]). It is also supported by the subcubic equivalence [WW10, VW18] between triangle detection and Boolean matrix multiplication.

**Determining whether a graph contains a dominated vertex:** A _dominated vertex_ is a node _x_ such that \(N(x)\subseteq N[y]\) for some \(y\neq x\). This problem turns out to be exactly equivalent to the Orthogonal Vectors (OV) problem in _n_ dimensions (see Section B in the appendix for a proof). Whether this high-dimensional OV problem requires fast matrix multiplication was first asked<sup>3</sup> almost 3 decades ago by Aingworth, Chekuri, Indyk and Motwani [ACIM99]. The hypothesis that OV in _n_ dimensions requires \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) time has been used in fine-grained complexity in recent years (see e.g., [DK21]).

**Determining whether a graph contains a simplicial vertex:** A node _v_ is _simplicial_ if **G**[_N(v_)] is a clique. The hypothesis that Simplicial Vertex requires \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) time has also been used in recent years for hardness results in fine-grained complexity (see e.g., [DJVW22]).

<sup>3</sup> They actually asked whether distinguishing between diameter 2 and 3 in an undirected graph in subcubic time without matrix multiplication, but this problem is easily seen to be equivalent to OV in _n_ dimensions, e.g., via a reduction as in [RV13, Vas18].

## 4 Asteroidal Triples and Friends in (Likely Necessary) Matrix Multiplication Time

OV and Triangle detection are central problems in fine-grained complexity. Simplicial Vertex has been used only a handful of times as a source of hardness. Nevertheless, it is a very natural problem. In fact, the three hard problems that Kratsch and Spinrad propose are just different quantifications of the following form:

\(Q_1x\in V,Q_2y\in N(x),Q_3z\in N(x):(y,z)\in E.\) (1)

Triangle detection has quantifiers \(Q_1Q_2Q_3=\exists\exists\exists\exists\) in Equation (1), Simplicial Vertex has \(Q_1Q_2Q_3=\exists\forall\forall\), and OV in _n_ dimensions (and dominated vertex) is equivalent to the case \(Q_1Q_2Q_3=\exists\exists\forall\) (this requires a bit of a proof since we need \(y\in N(x)\) - see Section B in the appendix). Kratsch and Spinrad [KS06] provide evidence that tight reductions between these different quantifications might be difficult due to an inherent difference in the non-deterministic complexity of the problems. Nevertheless, we do know that _fine-grained subcubic_ (but non-tight w.r.t. \(n^\omega\)) reductions exist from Simplicial Vertex and Dominated Vertex to Triangle Detection because both these problems can be solved using Boolean Matrix Multiplication (BMM) and BMM is fine-grained equivalent to Triangle Detection [WW10, VW18].

## Our Results

We show that all the problems presented by Spinrad and Kratsch can be solved in \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\) time. <sup>4</sup> Therefore, none of the presented problems fit into the aforementioned category of intermediate problems. If one is willing to believe that _n_-dimensional OV, Simplicial Vertex, and Triangle Detection all require \(n^{\omega-o(1)}\) time, then our algorithms are also optimal.

We start with neighborhood-deleted components, noting that this is equivalent to a more general problem that we call the _induced subgraph connected component_ problem: Given an _n_-vertex graph **G**=(_V,E_) and a family of subsets S of _V_ , compute the connected components of **G**[_S_] for each \(S\in\mathcal{S}\). This equivalence can easily be seen to hold for \(|\mathcal{S}|=\Theta(n)\): in one direction, we choose the sets to be the graphs obtained by deleting the (closed) neighborhoods; in the other direction, we introduce a clique containing one vertex for each \(S\in\mathcal{S}\), where each such vertex’s neighbors are exactly the vertices not in its corresponding set _S_.

We show that the induced subgraph connected component problem is _equivalent_ to multiplying an \(|\mathcal{S}|\times n\) Boolean matrix by an \(n\times n\) Boolean matrix. <sup>5</sup> This equivalence demonstrates that we can compute the connected components of multiple graphs more efficiently, provided they are all induced subgraphs of a single underlying graph.

**Main Theorem 1.** _There is a deterministic algorithm that solves the induced subgraph connected component problem in time_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\mathrm{MM}(|\mathcal{S}|,n,n))\) _for an n-node input graph and a non-empty input set_ S.

<sup>4</sup> To be precise, we show this for all problems in the journal version of [KS06]. The conference version contains one additional problem (finding clique cutsets) for which an \(\mathcal{O}(n^\omega)\)-time algorithm was found concurrently [HTV05]. Later, this result was extended to cliqueset decompositions in matrix multiplication time [CD18]. <sup>5</sup> We note that one (perhaps minor) reason we present this result for the induced subgraph connected component problem, as opposed to neighborhood deleted components, is that this equivalence with rectangular Boolean matrix product holds even when \(|\mathcal{S}|=\omega(n)\).

**Lemma 4.2.** _Given two Boolean matrices A and B of size_ \(s\times n\) _and_ \(n\times n\)_, one can construct in time_ O(_n_<sup>2</sup>+_ns_) _an instance of the induced subgraph connected component problem on a_ 2_n-node graph with a set of size s_=|S|_, such that solving this instance yields the product AB._

As a corollary to Main Theorem 1, we obtain algorithms for the following problems (for details on how the preceding algorithm implies these results, we refer the reader to [KS06, Corollaries 3.2, 3.3, and 3.4]).

**Corollary 1.1.** _The following problems have a deterministic_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\)_-time algorithm on an n-node input graph: computing neighborhood-deleted components in a graph, listing all extremities in a graph and determining whether the graph has a star cut-set, determining whether two fixed vertices x, y are a two-pair._

We also obtain an \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\)-time algorithm for recognizing AT-free graphs (a related result was previously known only for claw-free AT-free graphs in matrix multiplication time [HK02]), as well as for listing all dominating pairs and two-pairs.

**Main Theorem 2.** _There is a deterministic_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\)_-time algorithm that determines if a graph is AT-free._

Previously, the fastest time algorithm for recognizing AT-free graphs ran in O(_n_<sup>2.82</sup>) time [KS06].

**Main Theorem 3.** _There is a deterministic_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\)_-time algorithm for listing all dominating pairs._

This improves upon Spinrad and Kratsch’s O(_n_<sup>2.79</sup>) running time.

**Main Theorem 4.** _There is a deterministic_ \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\)_-time algorithm for listing all two-pairs._

The previous best running time was Spinrad and Kratsch’s O(_n_<sup>2.79</sup>).

We remark that all our algorithms are deterministic, and the underlying algorithms are remarkably simple. Although the algorithms themselves are straightforward, the proofs establishing their correctness are occasionally more complex (e.g., recognition of AT-free graphs); in such cases, the more involved proofs reveal new structural insights into the problems.

Finally, we study two related problems not addressed in the work of [KS06]. While we only achieve partial progress on these, we suspect their time complexity may strictly exceed \(\mathcal{O}(n^\omega)\). Their fine-grained complexity offers an interesting direction for future study, so we leave both problems open to the community.

**Induced Non-shortest Paths.** The first problem we propose is a generalization of verifying whether two vertices form a _two-pair_. More generally, given two vertices _u,v_ at distance _d(u,v_)=_k_, one can ask whether there exists an induced (equivalently, chordless) path between them that is not a shortest path (note that every shortest path is necessarily induced). Following previous work, we call such a path a _uv-trail_. In this terminology, the problem of listing two-pairs is the all-pairs version of this problem restricted to vertex pairs with _k_=2.

This problem is not new: it was recently introduced by Berger, Seymour, and Spirkl [BSS21], who gave an O(_n_<sup>18</sup>)-time algorithm for a single fixed pair. This was very recently improved by Chiu and Lu [CL24] to \(\mathcal{O}(n^{2\omega})\), i.e., the time required to multiply two \(n^2\times n^2\) matrices. No lower bound was provided, nor any evidence that matrix multiplication is necessary. We show that matrix multiplication seems necessary, even for a single pair with _k_=3, by giving a reduction from triangle detection.

**Lemma 4.16.** _For any_ \(k\ge 3\)_, suppose there exists an algorithm that, in time_ \(\mathsf{T}=\Omega(n^2)\)_, determines whether an n-node graph_ **G** _contains a uv-trail for two vertices u,v with d(u,v_)=_k. Then there is an algorithm solving triangle detection in time_ O(T).

## 6 Asteroidal Triples and Friends in (Likely Necessary) Matrix Multiplication Time

We find this problem interesting from a fine-grained complexity viewpoint because it appears closely related to another area whose fine-grained landscape still has many open problems: the detection of induced patterns (see \[FKLL12, VWWY15, BKS18, DVV21, DV22\]), where also runtimes of \(\mathcal{O}(n^{2\omega})\) are common, e.g., for detecting a six-clique or other patterns.

Finally, we mention that algorithms for detecting _uv_-trails have been used to improve the runtime for recognizing graphs in which all holes have the same length. This was first achieved by Cook et al. \[CHP<sup>+</sup>24\] in time O(_n_<sup>21</sup>) and subsequently improved by Chiu and Lu \[CL24\] to \(\mathcal{O}(n^{2\omega+3})\).

### Recognition of Quasi-Triangulated Graphs and Decremental Simplicial Vertex.

The second problem is the recognition of another generalization of triangulated graphs, called _quasi-triangulated_ graphs. A graph **G** is _quasi-triangulated_ if and only if every induced subgraph of **G** contains a simplicial vertex or a _cosimplicial vertex_ (i.e., a simplicial vertex in the complement). Just as triangulated graphs can be recognized by iteratively removing a simplicial vertex from the resulting graph, quasi-triangulated graphs can be recognized similarly by iteratively removing a simplicial or cosimplicial vertex. Thus both classes can be recognized using the following subroutine.

**Decremental Simplicial Vertex**

**Input:** An unweighted graph **G**=(_V,E_).

**Update:** Delete a given vertex _v_ together with all its incident edges.

**Query:** Does the current graph **G** contain a simplicial vertex? If so, return one.

Hence, to recognize whether a graph **G** is quasi-triangulated, it suffices to maintain a decremental simplicial vertex subroutine for both **G** and its complement \(\tilde{\mathbf{G}}\), proceeding iteratively as follows: In each iteration, check whether **G** or \(\tilde{\mathbf{G}}\) contains a simplicial vertex. If such a vertex _v_ exists in either graph, remove _v_ from both **G** and \(\tilde{\mathbf{G}}\). If this elimination process continues until the graph is empty, **G** is quasi-triangulated. Otherwise, if the process halts because neither **G** nor \(\tilde{\mathbf{G}}\) contains a simplicial vertex, the algorithm terminates and rejects **G**.

In reality, triangulated graphs can be recognized faster, in linear time \[RTL76\], using another simple algorithm. However, the fastest algorithm for quasi-triangulated graphs runs in time O(min(_n_<sup>2.77</sup>,_nm_)) \[Spi04, Hoà03\], where the recognition algorithm relies on the decremental simplicial vertex subroutine. We find this last problem especially interesting from a fine-grained point of view because edge- decremental triangle detection has recently been shown to admit a \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\)-time algorithm \[BBF<sup>+</sup>26\]. In this light, it would be interesting to see whether Triangle Detection, Simplicial Vertex, or High- dimensional OV all retain a \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\)-time algorithm, or whether some interesting difference emerges.

Our partial progress here is an improvement of the algorithm for Decremental Simplicial Vertex to O(_n_<sup>2.5275</sup>), which on sparse graphs can be balanced to be something slightly better.

**Theorem 4.14.** _There is an algorithm for Decremental Simplicial Vertex that on an n-node graph runs in time_

\(\mathcal{O}\left(min_{\Delta\in[1..n]}\left\{n/\Delta\cdot MM(n,\Delta,n)+m\cdot\Delta\right\}\right).\)

_In particular, with the current bounds on rectangular matrix multiplication_<sup>6</sup> _this gives a running time of_ O(_n_<sup>2.5275</sup>) _on dense graphs. For sparse graphs, bounding the rectangular product naively by dividing it into_ \(\Delta\times\Delta\) _blocks yields a running time of_ \(\mathcal{O}\left(m^{(3-\omega)/(4-\omega)}n^{3/(4-\omega)}\right)\).

Notably, the running time we obtain is the same as the best known running times for both directed unweighted APSP \[Zwi02\] and Min Witness Product \[CKL07\].

<sup>6</sup> We used the bounds from \[ADV<sup>+</sup>25\] plugged into van den Brand’s optimization tool \[Bra\].

## 2 Overview

In the following section, we give an overview of the proofs of Main Theorem 1, Main Theorem 2, and Main Theorem 3: the first because its proof is simple and can be explained briefly, and the second and third because they let us highlight the additional structural properties we establish for these problems.

### 2.1 Induced Subgraph Connected Components in Matrix Multiplication Time

Given a graph **G**=(_V,E_) and a family of subsets \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq 2^V\), our goal is to compute, for each \(S\in\mathcal{S}\), the connected components of **G**[_S_]. The core idea of the algorithm is to gradually grow the connected components of **G**[_S_] for every \(S\in\mathcal{S}\). We proceed in rounds, maintaining a partition of each **G**[_S_] that refines its connected components. Let _C<sub>S</sub>(u_) denote a unique identifier associated with the part containing node _u_ in **G**[_S_].

We initialize the process with singleton parts for the nodes in every **G**[_S_]. In each round, for every \(S\in\mathcal{S}\) and node \(u\in\mathbf{G}[S]\), we check whether there exists an edge \(\{u,w\}\in\mathbf{G}[S]\) such that \(C_S(u)\neq C_S(w)\). Discovering such an edge allows us to merge the respective parts and update \(C_S(\cdot)\) accordingly for each _S_. We claim that O(log_n_) rounds suffice for these partitions to grow into the connected components. Indeed, any part that does not yet form a complete connected component will, by induction, contain at least 2_<sup>i</sup>_ nodes after the _i_-th round.

It remains to briefly outline how to find the edges across which we merge parts. We accomplish this in parallel for each **G**[_S_] via matrix multiplication. To this end, in each round we assign every part in each **G**[_S_] a value of zero or one, chosen uniformly and independently at random. Let \(C'_S(u)\) denote the bit assigned to the part _C<sub>S</sub>(u_).

Note that if, for some \(S\in\mathcal{S}\) and \(u\in\mathbf{G}[S]\), there exists an edge \(\{u,w\}\in\mathbf{G}[S]\) with \(C_S(u)\neq C_S(w)\), then with probability 1/4 we have \(C'_S(u)=0\) and \(C'_S(w)=1\). Furthermore, edges contained entirely within a single part of **G**[_S_] always have their endpoints assigned the same bit. Thus, it suffices to search for an edge spanning parts with differing assigned bits, repeating the procedure a logarithmic number of times to guarantee success with high probability.

The product we perform is between an \(|\mathcal{S}|\times n\) Boolean matrix _M_ (indexed by the sets in S and the vertices in _V_ ) and the adjacency matrix _A_ of **G** (indexed by the vertices in _V_ ). For the matrix _M_, we set _MS<sub>S,w</sub>=_1 if and only if \(w\in\mathbf{G}[S]\) and \(C'_S(w)=1\). It is easy to see that for every \(S\in\mathcal{S}\) and \(u\in\mathbf{G}[S]\) with \(C'_S(u)=0\), there exists an inter-part edge {_u,w_} if and only if (_MA)<sub>S,u</sub>=_1. The Boolean matrix multiplication witness for this product directly provides the desired edge.

It is also not difficult to derandomize the above procedure. In the full proof, we provide such a derandomized version with a slightly more formal presentation.

### 2.2 Recognizing AT-free Graphs in Matrix Multiplication Time

We proceed to outline the main idea behind our \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\omega_0})\)-time algorithm to verify whether a graph **G**=(_V,E_) contains an AT. We recall that such a triple consists of an independent set \(\{x,y,z\}\subseteq V\) such that there exists a path between every pair of nodes in {_x,y,z_} that does not pass through the neighborhood of the third node.

Before presenting the main idea of the algorithm, we note that the triangle-detection hardness of finding such a triple can be shown to rely solely on the condition that \(\{x,y,z\}\subseteq V\) forms an independent set. To clarify our point, we consider the following elementary reduction demonstrating how, given a tripartite graph \(\mathbf{G}=(X\cup Y\cup Z,E)\), we can build a graph \(\mathbf{G}'=(V',E')\) such that **G** contains a triangle

{_x,y,z_} if and only if \(\mathbf{G}'\) contains an AT \(\{x',y',z'\}^7\) (see Figure 2a). To achieve this, it suffices to invert all edges in **G** (including those within _X,Y_ , and _Z_ , which consequently become cliques) and add three new vertices _a,b,c_ that are fully connected to \(X\cup Z\), \(Y\cup Z\), and \(X\cup Y\) , respectively. We also add the edges {_a,b_}, {_b,c_}, and {_c,a_}. It is easy to see that \(\mathbf{G}'\) satisfies the claimed property. However, notice that for every triple with \(x\in X\), \(y\in Y\) , and \(z\in Z\) , there is always an _x-y_ path avoiding _N[z_] (and similarly for the other pairs). ## 2.3 Listing Dominating Pairs in Matrix Multiplication Time

Next, we turn to listing all dominating pairs _u,v_ of an input graph **G**. Recall that _u,v_ form a dominating pair if every _u-v_ path is a dominating set, and recall that _C<sub>x</sub>(y_) denotes the connected component containing _y_ in **G**_<sub>x</sub>_. The connection between this problem and neighborhood-deleted components is that _u,v_ is _not_ a dominating pair if and only if there is some node \(w\notin N[u]\cup N[v]\) such that _C<sub>w</sub>(u_)=_C<sub>w</sub>(v_); that is, there exists a _u-v_ path avoiding the neighborhood of _w_. In such a case, we say that the component _C<sub>w</sub>(u_)=_C<sub>w</sub>(v_) _witnesses_ the non-dominating pair _u,v_.

Following this logic, a naive algorithm would simply iterate over each \(v\in V\) , examine each connected component _C_ of **G**_<sub>v</sub>_, and mark all pairs of distinct nodes _x_, \(y\in C\) as non-dominating. We note that for a subset C of connected components (potentially spanning different **G**_<sub>v</sub>_), we can implement this in time O(MM(_n,_|C|_,n_)). To achieve this, it suffices to construct an \(n\times|\mathcal{C}|\) matrix _M_, indexed by vertices in _V_ and components in C respectively, with _M_<sub>_v,C_</sub>=1 if \(v\in C\). The Boolean product \(MM^\top\) indicates exactly when a pair _u,v_ is witnessed as non-dominating by some component in C, which occurs precisely when \((MM^\top)_{u,v}=1\). Kratsch and Spinrad’s approach distinguishes between large components, which contain at least \(\Delta\) nodes, and small ones. Since there can be at most \(n^2/\Delta\) of the former across all **G**_<sub>v</sub>_, marking all their pairs as non-dominating via the matrix method takes \(MM(n,n^2/\Delta,n)=\mathcal{O}(n^{\omega+1}/\Delta)\) time. They also show how to process small components in \(\mathcal{O}(n^2\cdot\Delta)\) time; balancing these two bounds yields an overall running time of \(\mathcal{O}(n^{(\omega+3)/2})\).

Our algorithm differs in two ways:

1 Instead of collecting into the set C all connected components above a threshold size \(\Delta\), we include only the largest connected component from each **G**_<sub>v</sub>_. By doing so, it takes only \(\mathcal{O}(n^\omega)\) time to find all non-dominating pairs witnessed by these components.

On the other hand, for non-dominating pairs that have no witness in C, we prove an interesting structural result: if _u,v_ has no "large" witness, then it must have many witnesses. More specifically, we prove that if _u,v_ is a non-dominating pair witnessed by some \(C\notin\mathcal{C}\) in **G**_<sub>x</sub>_, then there are at least \(\Omega(|V\backslash N[x]|)\) nodes \(y\in V\) such that **G**_<sub>y</sub>_ contains a component witnessing _u,v_. Assuming for simplicity that |_N[x_]|=_o(n_) for all \(x\in V\) , we can exploit this property as follows: we sample \(\Theta(logn)\) nodes and, for each sampled node _y_, find all non-dominating pairs witnessed by any component of **G**_<sub>y</sub>_. This takes O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) time per sampled node _y_, since the sizes of the components in each **G**_<sub>y</sub>_ sum to O(_n_).

## Open Problems

To conclude this section, we list some other open problems:

First, we report an open problem posed in [KS06]. It is well established that every AT-free graph contains a dominating pair [COS97], which can, in fact, be found in linear time [COS99]. However, neither AT-free graph recognition nor finding a dominating pair in a general graph can be solved in linear time unless \(\omega=2\) or some fine-grained complexity hypothesis fails. This leads to an interesting open question: is there a robust, linear-time algorithm for finding a dominating pair in an AT-free graph? Here, "robust" is used in the sense of [RS03]; a robust linear-time algorithm must take an arbitrary (i.e., not necessarily AT-free) graph as input and, in linear time, either output a dominating pair or correctly report that the graph is not AT-free.

We showed that detecting an AT-triple has the same time complexity as detecting a triangle in a graph. In time \(\mathcal{O}(n^\omega)\), however, we can solve problems stronger than triangle detection, e.g., the all-edge triangle problem, where for each edge we want to know whether it is contained in a triangle. Our approach for detecting an AT-triple does not seem to yield such an all-edge version in \(\mathcal{O}(n^\omega)\) time, and the latter seems considerably more difficult: namely, for each pair _x_, _y_ we want to know whether there is a _z_ such that {_x,y,z_} is an AT. It would be interesting to determine whether a running time of \(\mathcal{O}(n^\omega)\) is achievable, or whether some hardness result rules this out.

Generally, there is a plethora of other important structures in structural graph theory that admit polynomial-time algorithms which are nonetheless clearly far from optimal, where a fine-grained complexity lens could help uncover new structural properties; see, e.g., perfect graphs [CLV03, CKS05] or graphs with even or odd holes [CL15, CSSS20, CLL22].

### Deterministic Fingerprints for Partitions.

Suppose we are given a graph **G**=(_V,E_) and a family of vertex sets \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq 2^V\). Further, let _C<sub>S</sub>(v_) be the connected component of \(v\in V\) in **G**\[_S_\]. To quickly check whether \(C_S(v)=C_{S^\prime}(v')\) for distinct \(v,v'\in V\) and \(S,S'\in\mathcal{S}\), we introduce the following fingerprints for the connected components.

**Lemma 3.2.** _Consider a set V_=\[1_..n_\] _together with k partitions_ P<sub>1</sub>_,...,_P_<sub>k</sub> of V, and for_ \(v\in V\) _let P<sub>i</sub>(v_) _denote the set of the i-th partition containing v. Then, in deterministic time_ O(_nk_log(_nk_))_, we can construct functions_ \(h_1,\dots,h_k:V\rightarrow[1..M]\) _with M=_O(_nk_) _that assigns a_ fingerprint _to each set of each partition, such that h<sub>i</sub>(v_)=_h<sub>j</sub>(u_) _if and only if P<sub>i</sub>(v_)=_P<sub>j</sub>(u)._

**Proof.** Let \(\mathcal{P}=\sqcup_{i=1}^k\mathcal{P}_i\) be the multiset containing all sets. We proceed as follows.

**Our algorithm.** First, we sort the elements of each set \(P\in\mathcal{P}\), looking at them as lists. Equal lists have equal size, so we partition P into buckets by length; lists in different buckets get different fingerprints. Within a bucket \(\mathcal{P}^\ell\subseteq\mathcal{P}\) all lists have length \(\ell\), and we sort them lexicographically, making equal lists adjacent. A single scan then assigns fingerprints by incrementing a global counter whenever the current list differs from its predecessor, and we store _h<sub>i</sub>(v_) as the fingerprint of _P<sub>i</sub>(v_) in a table indexed by \([1..k]\times V\) . It is not difficult to see that this construction satisfies the claimed property.

**Runtime.** Sorting sets initially, bucketing by lengths, and the final scan cost at most O(_nk_log_n_).

For the lexicographic sort on \(\mathcal{P}^\ell\) we use \(\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{P}^\ell|\mathrm{log}|\mathcal{P}^\ell|)\) comparisons, where each comparison costs \(\mathcal{O}(\ell)\) time. Overall this costs \(\mathcal{O}(\sum_{\ell=1}^n\ell\cdot|\mathcal{P}^\ell|\mathrm{log}|\mathcal{P}^\ell|)=\mathcal{O}(nk\mathrm{log}(nk))\), because the sizes of the lists sum up to _nk_ and \(|\mathcal{P}^\ell|=\mathcal{O}(nk)\); empty buckets contribute zero.

## 4.2 Recognizing AT-free Graphs in Matrix Multiplication Time

In this section, we present an \(\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^\omega)\)-time algorithm for recognizing AT-free graphs. To achieve this, we first introduce a helpful relationship between neighborhood-deleted components that share the same vertices across different **G**_<sub>x</sub>_.

**Proposition 4.3.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be an undirected graph. Consider a vertex_ \(x\in V\) _and two vertices_ \(a,b\in\mathbf{G}_x\) _such that a and b belong to distinct neighborhood-deleted components of x, i.e.,_ \(C_x(a)\neq C_x(b)\)_. The following conditions are equivalent:_

(1) _The neighborhood-deleted component containing a is identical in_ **G**_<sub>x</sub> and_ **G**_<sub>b</sub>, i.e.,_ \(C_x(a)=C_b(a)\).

(2) _The neighborhood N(b_) _contains the neighborhood of_ \(C_x(a)\).

**Proof.** We first observe that \(C_x(a)\subseteq C_b(a)\) always holds. Since \(C_x(a)\neq C_x(b)\), no vertex in \(C_x(a)\) is adjacent to _b_; thus, \(N[b]\cap C_x(a)=\varnothing\) and all paths within \(C_x(a)\) remain intact in **G**_<sub>b</sub>_.

## A Motivation for the Kratsch-Spinrad problems

Almost all the structures considered by Spinrad and Kratsch are fundamental to structural graph theory. They are closely intertwined and can be understood through four central graph classes:

The first class consists of _perfect graphs_, defined as graphs where every induced subgraph has a chromatic number equal to the size of its maximum clique. Perfect graphs are best known for the Strong Perfect Graph Theorem, conjectured by Berge in the 1960s [Ber60, Ber61] and proven by Chudnovsky, Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas [CRST06]. In this context, _star-cutsets_ were first introduced by Chvátal [Chv85] to characterize minimal imperfect graphs, establishing star- cutsets as a powerful structural obstruction used to decompose graph classes and prove perfection [Chv85, Ree87].

_Triangulated graphs_ (also called _chordal, rigid-circuit, monotone transitive_, or _perfect elimination_ graphs) are graphs in which every cycle of length four or more has a chord. Dirac [Dir61] gave two equivalent characterizations: a graph is chordal if and only if every induced subgraph is either a clique or contains two non-adjacent _simplicial vertices_ or, equivalently, if and only if every minimal cutset is a _clique-cutset_. The latter formulation highlights why many problems can be solved faster on chordal graphs [Gav72, RTL76]: a clique cutset decomposes a graph into independently solvable pieces, since the separating clique interacts uniformly with every part of the split. This property of clique cutsets can be exploited for other graph classes as well.

A superclass of triangulated graphs is the class of _weakly triangulated graphs_, in which _two-pairs_ play a fundamental role. Weakly triangulated graphs were first defined by Hayward [Hay85] as graphs containing no induced _holes_ (that is, induced cycles of length at least five) or _antiholes_ (holes in the complement). Note that this is a generalization of triangulated graphs, since forbidding induced cycles of length four and five already forbids all antiholes. Sritharan conjectured that weakly triangulated graphs are exactly the graphs in which every induced subgraph is either a complete graph or contains a two-pair (so two-pairs play a role analogous to that of simplicial vertices). This was later proven by Chvátal and Rusu [CR93] (see also [ES95, CRS02]). Two-pairs are also central in the design of efficient algorithms for weakly triangulated graphs [HHM90, HSS07].

Last but not least, _AT-free_ graphs were first introduced by Lekkerkerker and Boland [LB62] as a way to relate interval graphs and triangulated graphs: they showed that a graph is an interval graph if and only if it is both chordal and AT-free. AT-free graphs were subsequently studied in relation to other graph classes, such as cocomparability graphs and perfect graphs [Gal67, LB79, GMT84], before being investigated in their own right in the seminal work of Corneil, Olariu, and Stewart [COS97]. One property of interval graphs that [COS97] extended to AT-free graphs is that every such graph contains a _dominating pair_ realizing the diameter. These and other properties of AT-free graphs allow several NP-hard problems to be solved in polynomial time on AT-free graphs (e.g., [Sta12, KM12, BKKM99, Kra00, KMT08]); moreover, recent algorithmic results on AT-free graphs have even achieved running times that bypass the fine-grained lower bounds [Duc22, DDHV25].

## B Dominated vertex is equivalent to OV

Recall that a vertex _u_ in a graph **G** is dominated by a node _v_ if every neighbor of _u_ is also a neighbor of _v_ or is _v_. We will present two reductions. The first will reduce the problem of finding a dominated vertex to OV in _n_ dimensions. The second will reduce the OV problem to finding a dominated vertex in a given graph. We will then conclude with a short extra proof, that OV in _n_ dimensions is equivalent to Dominated vertex which is also equivalent to solving \(\exists x\in V,\exists y\in N(v),\forall z\in N(v),(y,z)\in E\).

**Lemma B.1.** _Given an n-node graph_ **G**=(_V,E_) _one can create in_ O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) _time an instance of OV on two sets of n vectors on_ 2_n dimensions so that it has a pair of orthogonal vectors if and only if G has a dominated vertex._

**Proof.** Let _A_ be the \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix of **G** and let _C_ be its complement. Let _I_ be the \(n\times n\) identity matrix. Let _X_ be the \(n\times 2n\) matrix obtained by concatenating _A_ and _I_ (with _I_ to the right of _A_). Now let _Y_ be the \(2n\times n\) matrix obtained by concatenating _C_ on top of _I_.

Note that for any given \(i,j\in[n]\), we have that (_XY_)[_i,j_]=0 iff

for every _k_ such that \((i,k)\in E\), we have \((k,j)\in E\) (i.e. if _A[i,k_]=1, then _C[k,j_]=0), and

also \(i\neq j\) (i.e. \(I[i,i]\cdot I[i,j]=0\)).

Note that the standard reduction from OV on two sets to OV on a single set still works here: you can create a single \(2n\times(2n+2)\) matrix, _Z_, by concatenating _X_ on top of the complement of _Y_ and add two new columns, so that every row in _Z_ corresponding to a row of _X_ has 01 in those two columns, and every row in _Z_ corresponding to a column of _Y_ has 10 in those two columns.

Now we give the second direction of the reduction.
